item.title: From seed to plate at East Wiltshire Intermediate School
item.description:
From seed to plate at East Wiltshire Intermediate School jenniferdhogan Thu, 10/29/2026 - 13:16

Students in the foods and nutrition class at East Wiltshire Intermediate in Cornwall aren’t just learning how to cook; they’re learning where their food comes from.

As part of the provincial curriculum and through the school's garden project, students are developing a deeper connection to food and the environment around them, by planting, harvesting, and preparing a variety of fruits, vegetables, and herbs in a garden in the school's backyard.

The project has been growing since 2022, providing many students with the chance to step outside the traditional classroom setting and engage with food production from seed to plate.

Sarah McIntosh is the Foods and Nutrition teacher in the Life Skills Program and one of three staff members who share the leadership responsibilities of the garden.

“Whether students are planting seeds in the spring, harvesting squash in the fall, or just taking the time to observe the evolving cycles of the garden, it creates a lot of curiosity in them,” she said.

“It’s been great for giving students ideas and experiences with hands-on cooking, creating, and tasting. It gives them a broader perspective on flavours, and what can be done locally as well.”

In the foods class, as part of the provincial curriculum, McIntosh teaches students how to make recipes that feature fresh veggies and herbs, such as bruschetta, zucchini egg muffins, pickled beans, breakfast burritos, and warming soups in the fall.

For Grade 8 student Ryan Rix, one of the highlights has been harvesting ingredients that later become part of their meals in class.

"I like working in the garden," he said. "My favourite part is probably just coming outside to pick veggies for the food we make."

One of his favourite meals included fresh parsley, green onions, and chives from the garden.

The project has helped students develop practical gardening skills, like learning how to tell when vegetables are ready to be harvested.

"The skills I've learned are knowing the right time to pick the veggies in the garden," he said. "It teaches you if they are good to eat yet or not."

For Grade 8 student Cole Rix, working in the garden has given him a new appreciation for the time and effort involved in growing food.

"It takes a lot of time for them to grow," he said. "You just have to use a lot of water and then wait."

Rix says the garden has encouraged him to eat healthier food and try new things.

"I tried peppers from the garden this year and I've never tried them before, and they actually tasted pretty good," he said.

The impact of the garden extends far beyond the harvest. It serves as an outdoor classroom for science lessons, offers hands-on learning opportunities for students in the resource area, and provides meaningful garden-based activities for students receiving behavioral support.

McIntosh hopes other Island schools will be encouraged to start gardens in their school communities.

 "We hope to increase community involvement to create meaningful relationships with our nearby neighbours and to help manage the needs of the garden over summer break," she said.

For students like Ryan, the garden has changed the way he thinks about food and fresh ingredients.

 "The fresher it is, it really tastes better, rather than buying something, it tastes a lot better just growing it yourself."

The East Wiltshire Intermediate School garden project was made possible by the province’s Outdoor Learning Grant, which is offered to K-12 educators in Prince Edward Island. The grant empowers educators to create hands-on outdoor learning experiences that enrich the curriculum and foster environmental stewardship.

item.title: Project Red Ribbon Day raising awareness about impaired driving
item.description:
Project Red Ribbon Day raising awareness about impaired driving jenniferdhogan Thu, 10/29/2026 - 10:49

As part of MADD Canada’s Project Red Ribbon Day, public safety officials, RCMP members and MADD Canada volunteers will conduct roadside checkpoints and distribute red ribbons and educational materials on November 1 to raise awareness about impaired driving.

The roadside checkpoints and mandatory alcohol screenings will take place at Nabuurs Garden in Montague at 1 p.m. and Jewell’s Country Market in Marshfield at 4 p.m. on November 1. 

“The devastating effects of impaired driving are far reaching. Campaigns like Project Red Ribbon Day play a vital role in making our roads safer by raising awareness about the dangers of impaired driving. Islanders are encouraged to display a red ribbon as a reminder of the importance of sober driving and making responsible decisions.”

-Transportation and Infrastructure Minister Bloyce Thompson

The Project Red Ribbon Day Act received Royal Assent in 2025, making Prince Edward Island the first jurisdiction in Canada to formally establish the day through legislation. 

The day recognizes the devastating impact of impaired driving and honours those who have been killed or injured as a result.

“Prince Edward Island has made history by recognizing the importance of Project Red Ribbon Day, particularly as we approach the holiday season, when it is essential to remind everyone to plan ahead and never drive impaired,” said CEO of MADD Canada Steve Sullivan. “We hope PEI’s leadership inspires other provinces and territories to follow suit. By working together to promote sober driving and responsible choices, we can help prevent deaths and injuries and ensure everyone gets home safely.”

item.title: Marion L. Reid Grant helping build PEI's health care workforce
item.description:
Marion L. Reid Grant helping build PEI's health care workforce jenniferdhogan Thu, 10/29/2026 - 10:12

More Islanders are pursuing careers in health care through the Marion L. Reid Grant, helping address workforce needs across Prince Edward Island's health system.

Today, 176 students are receiving support through the grant, and 32 graduates are already working in health care professions across the province. Grant recipients are studying and working in a range of high-demand fields, including nursing, social work, pharmacy, physiotherapy and medical imaging. 

“Every health care worker starts out as a student with a goal of making a difference. The Marion L. Reid Grant helps students access the education and training they need while encouraging them to build their careers here in PEI. By supporting local talent, we are strengthening the workforce Islanders rely on and improving access to care across the province.” 

- Minister of Health and Wellness Cory Deagle

Launched in 2024, the Marion L. Reid Grant provides eligible students with $3,500 a year for up to four academic years, for a maximum of $14,000, while they complete studies in one of 17 eligible health care programs at designated universities and colleges across Canada. Recipients commit to working in PEI's health system for two years after graduation. In 2025-26, the province increased the annual grant amount and expanded eligibility to include occupational therapy, physiotherapy, paramedicine and dentistry.

"The Marion L. Reid Grant helps remove financial barriers for students while creating clear pathways into rewarding health care careers in Prince Edward Island," said Minister of Workforce and Advanced Learning Jenn Redmond. "By supporting Islanders throughout their education and encouraging them to build their careers here at home, we are investing in both student success and the future of our health care workforce."

Named in honour of Prince Edward Island's first female Lieutenant-Governor, Marion L. Reid, the grant reflects her legacy of public service by supporting Islanders pursuing careers dedicated to caring for others. 

The grant is part of a broader provincial commitment to improving access to care by expanding educational opportunities for Islanders pursuing careers in health care. 

Through initiatives such as the Healthcare Priorities Program, which has provided free tuition to more than 800 Islanders in resident care work, licensed practical nursing and paramedicine programs through a $10 million investment, and ongoing support for the UPEI Faculty of Medicine, the province is helping more Islanders access the education and training needed to build health care careers at home while supporting the future needs of communities across Prince Edward Island.

Together, these investments are creating stronger pathways from education and training to careers in the Island’s health system, helping grow the workforce and improve timely, high-quality access to care for Islanders now and in the years ahead.

item.title: Premier McLeod on the Enbridge Line 21 Pipeline
item.description:
YELLOWKNIFE - Premier Bob McLeod issued the following statement on the Enbridge Line 21 pipeline today:

“I was pleased to learn that operations have resumed for Enbridge’s Line 21 pipeline after almost 2 years of no activity.

"Resource development has, and will continue to be, the backbone of our economy and is central to ensuring a good source of middle class jobs and business opportunities. Our territory has mineral and petroleum resources and the development of those resources can have a transformative effect on our people and economy.

"Sustainable economic development is key to the future of Northerners. With a strong resource development base, we will be able to support diversification of our local economies into emerging and established sectors.

"On behalf of the Government of the Northwest Territories I’d like to offer my congratulations to Imperial Oil, Enbridge the town of Norman Wells and other partners for getting this pipeline back up and running. I know the efforts and economic impacts of the pipeline have already begun to take shape in the community and will be felt for years to come. ”

 

Charlotte Digness
Media and Communications Coordinator
Cabinet Communications and Protocol
Government of the Northwest Territories
